seo.title: Karmic tail 21 4 10 compatibility: an empire by the blue sea
seo.description: Karmic tail 21 4 10 compatibility: The World at the entry, The Emperor in the middle, The Wheel of Fortune as the main task, read through a famous fairy tale.

title: The 21-4-10 karmic tail in a couple's compatibility: an empire by the blue sea
short: The 21-4-10 karmic tail in compatibility opens with the card that, for Waite, closes the journey of the Major Arcana: The World — fullness, everything at once. It ends with The Wheel of Fortune, a card that belongs to no one. Between them sits The Emperor. The couple's story reads almost without translation: two people want a whole world together, build an empire for it out of order, rules and roles along the way, and run into the main thing — life turns without asking their permission. The story was written down long ago, and most people know it from childhood: it is the tale of the fisherman and the fish.

sections.h2: A fairy tale with the three cards in order
paragraphs: Pushkin finished "The Tale of the Fisherman and the Fish" on 14 October 1833 at Boldino. He took the plot from the Brothers Grimm: in their collection the tale is number 19 and is called "Von dem Fischer un syner Fru" — "The Fisherman and His Wife". The painter Philipp Otto Runge wrote it down in the Low German dialect of Pomerania. Pushkin made everything Russian and cut one thing: in his draft, after becoming tsaritsa, the old woman demands to be made "Roman pope" and sits at the top of the Tower of Babel. The German text is quoted below in Margaret Hunt's 1884 translation unless marked otherwise.

In the German original the ladder is longer and more candid. The fisherman's wife lives in a hovel, then wants a cottage, then a stone castle, then to be King, then **Emperor — Kaiser**, then Pope. And the last wish is **to be like God, so as to order the sun and the moon to rise herself**. After that, everything goes back to the hovel.
Lay the tale beside the tail and the match is almost mechanical:

ul: **The World.** The open sea and a question that can be answered with anything at all: "What is it you want, old man?" The whole world at their disposal.
**The Emperor.** A ladder of ranks: noblewoman, tsaritsa, King, Kaiser. In the palace, boyars, guards with axes, servants who get beaten.
**The Wheel of Fortune.** The wish to own luck itself — to have the fish "run her errands", to have the sun rise on command. And a turn back, exactly to where they began.

paragraphs: One more detail, without which the tale would be no use for talking about a couple. This is not a story of meeting. The old man and his wife had lived together "exactly thirty years and three" (Pushkin, our translation). It is the story of a long marriage in which, suddenly, a chance appears to get everything.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: a sea that needs nothing
paragraphs: The entry point of a couple's tail is what the two want together: shared wishes, agreements, a common language. In Lisovskaya's book The World in a couple means people with a similar philosophy of life — free, quick to set off, "the ideal couple" in many eyes; they are easy to talk to, and they split everything in half. The 21-4-10 tail starts with exactly that kind of wish: to have everything, all at once, whole, with no rough corners. A flat where every shelf is thought through. A holiday where every interest lines up. A life with no "we haven't got round to it yet".

The tale's first scene is The World in its purest form. The old man pulls in his net with the golden fish, hears the promise of any ransom he likes, and refuses: "I have no need of your ransom; / Off you go into the blue sea, / Roam there freely in the open" (Pushkin, our translation). In the German text his answer to his wife is even shorter: "What should I wish for?" Open space that need not be owned — that is The World when it stands in its positive aspect.

But the entry point stands on the line of tasks, and Lisovskaya warns that the same wish can become resistance. In the tale it does. This couple's wish is not shared. One needs nothing, the other needs everything. And it shows in the main clue of the German text — the spell the fisherman uses to call the fish. He says it six times, each time in the same words:
Manntje, Manntje, Timpe Te, / Buttje, Buttje in der See, / myne Fru de Ilsebill / will nich so as ik wol will.

The first two lines are a sound-spell, a call: "Little man, little man… little flounder, little flounder in the sea." The last two mean, literally: **"My wife Ilsebill wants not the way I want"** (our translation). This couple's common language is a formula of disagreement. And it is said not to the wife, but to the fish: to a third party who has the power to grant.

In real life it looks nothing like a fairy tale. The couple's wishes get discussed with anyone except each other: with a friend, with Mum, in the work chat. "She wants more again." "He never wants anything." The one who "wants nothing" seems more modest, but takes part all the same: by refusing to wish, they hand the couple's whole wish to the other. And a wish carried alone only grows upward. The roles are not split by gender: in the tale it is the wife who dreams, but in a living couple it can be either of the two — and they often swap places.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: a ladder where each is a head shorter
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya's book the middle of the tail has no meaning of its own — it is an addition to the main task. We read it as the road: what the couple does on the way from the wish to the trial. For the 21-4-10 couple, The Emperor stands on that road, and the road is a building site.

In the Grimms' tale every step is described with an accountant's precision. The cottage has a porch, a parlour and bedroom, a kitchen and pantry, things made of tin and brass, hens, ducks and a little garden. The castle has a marble hall, crystal chandeliers, stables, a park half a mile long. When the wife becomes King, her maids-in-waiting stand in a row on both sides of the throne, **"each of them always one head shorter than the last"**. When she becomes Emperor, the throne is made of one piece of gold two miles high, she holds the sceptre in one hand and the imperial orb in the other, and on both sides stand two rows of guards lined up by height, "from the biggest giant, who was two miles high, to the very smallest dwarf, just as big as my little finger". When she becomes Pope, there are two rows of candles, "the largest of which was as tall as the very tallest tower, down to the very smallest kitchen candle". The Emperor's order is drawn here literally: a world where everyone has a place and each place is one step smaller than the next.

The most important thing on this ladder happens to the word "we". The wife asks for the cottage and the castle for the two of them. Next morning in the castle she pokes her husband with her elbow and says: "Look you, couldn't we be the King over all that land?" He answers that he does not want to be King. And then it comes: "Well, if you won't be King, I will." From that moment the wife says only "I": "I will", "I must", "I am King". In the cottage and in the castle she took her husband by the hand and led him in. In the King's palace there is no hand any more: the fisherman walks in alone, stops before the high throne and looks up at his wife.

Then the fisherman says the sentence that holds the couple's whole Emperor: **"There is only one Emperor in the land"** — in the original "Kaiser is man eenmal im Reich", an empire has one emperor. The wife's answer is just as short: "I am the King, and you are nothing but my husband." Pushkin says the same in Russian terms: the new noblewoman sends her husband to serve in the stable, at the tsaritsa's court the boyars shove him out by the scruff, the guards nearly cut him down with their axes, and the people laugh: "Don't sit in a sledge that isn't yours!" — a Russian proverb for knowing one's place (our translation).

Waite himself remarks that this card and that of the Empress "do not precisely represent the condition of married life, though this state is implied". In a couple's tail this distinction becomes the theme: The Emperor is marriage not as a feeling but as a structure. In Lisovskaya's book The Emperor in a couple means reliability, a safety net, "measure twice, cut once", shared plans; in the negative — decisions made for everyone, nitpicking, rules that later get in the way of the very people who made them, and a struggle for leadership. Her advice is to divide areas of responsibility instead of competing over who is in charge.

In a modern couple the ladder looks like this. First a rented flat, then their own, then a house, then a second house or a joint business. Every step is a victory, and every victory becomes the floor from which the next one is measured. A spending spreadsheet appears, and one day it turns into an instrument of control. A rule appears — "this is how we do things" — and a couple of years later nobody remembers why it was introduced. A question appears: who decides about the car, the renovation, holidays and children? And if there is one answer to all of it, the realm once again has a single Kaiser.

The numbers add a clue the tale does not have. **In such a couple, neither of the two has The Emperor in the middle of their personal tail.** The couple's 4 always comes from 31: from The Sun and The Hanged Man (19 + 12), from The Tower and The Devil (16 + 15) or from The Hermit and The Fool (9 + 22). The empire is not brought in by one person — two people build it. And in each of the three pairs of middles, one card throws things open — The Sun, The Tower, The Fool — and the other holds on — The Hanged Man, The Devil, The Hermit. That is our reading, but the tale shows the same pair of forces from both sides: one keeps wanting to go further, the other keeps wanting to stop.

sections.h2: Main task: a sunrise no one can command
paragraphs: In Lisovskaya's book the couple's main task is read mostly through the negative: what is not working for the two and what they need to learn. The key word of her chapter on The Wheel of Fortune is cyclicity: rises and crises in a couple follow one another, and it is the alternation itself that has to be accepted, not fought. In the negative, The Wheel means a "silence — conflict" seesaw, "hard together, yet something holds us", blaming fate and each other, letting problems drift.

The tale takes this to the limit. Having become Pope, the fisherman's wife cannot sleep: she keeps thinking what else she could become, and can think of nothing. At dawn she sees the sun rising through the window, and it comes to her. In Hunt's translation: "if I can't order the sun and moon to rise, and have to look on and see the sun and moon rising, I can't bear it. I shall not know what it is to have another happy hour". What is unbearable is not poverty, not cramped rooms, not the husband. **What is unbearable is watching something turn on its own.** That is The Wheel of Fortune in a single sentence. In Pushkin the same wish takes a sea metaphor: to become "sovereign of the sea", so that the golden fish — luck in person — would "run her errands" (our translation).

For Waite, the Wheel stands for "the perpetual motion of a fluidic universe and for the flux of human life". And in passing he mocks the occult explanations claiming that the card means "principle, fecundity, virile honour, **ruling authority**" — among other things, the power of a ruler; he calls them "of a singularly fatuous kind". For the 21-4-10 couple this is a direct hit. Their main task keeps asking to be read in the language of their middle — as a question of power over the turn. Yet the Wheel, for Waite, does not reduce to power even in theory. Wen says the same in practical terms: upright, the Seeker's life "is going with the flow of the wheel", and the card itself can mean a "matter beyond the Seeker's control".

Now the main secret of this tail. The tale is usually read as the story of a greedy old woman and a kind old man. But in the Grimms' version the old man cannot bear the Wheel either — only from the other side. At every step he says the same thing. In the cottage: "Let it stay so; now we will live content" (our translation). In the castle: "now let it be; and we will live in this beautiful castle and be content". Before the King: "now we will wish for nothing more". Before the Pope: "be satisfied, you cannot become anything greater now". Pushkin strikes the same note: "Surely now your little soul is content" (our translation). And each time the wife answers: "We will think about that" — "Dat wähl wy uns bedenken".

One wants to stop the wheel on the spoke where things are good right now. The other wants to turn it herself. These are two ways of refusing the turn: to freeze it and to command it. That is why the 21-4-10 couple quarrels not about money and not about power, though the words will be about those. **It quarrels about time.** One says "let's not change anything", the other says "let's change everything, and now". One holds on to the step, the other strains towards the next. And the wheel turns at the word of neither.

In the tale the Wheel does not turn suddenly. It gives warning — and this is perhaps the most useful clue for a living couple. In Pushkin the sea changes with every trip the old man makes, and it is worth rereading exactly how it is written: "He sees the sea has grown a little rough", then "(The blue sea has grown cloudy.)", "(The blue sea is restless.)", "(The blue sea has turned black.)" and finally "a black storm on the sea" (our translation). Pushkin put three states of the sea in brackets. **The signals stand in brackets** — like a stage direction that nobody in the tale answers.

In the Grimms' version the scale is even more detailed. First the water is "all green and yellow, and no longer so smooth", then "quite purple and dark-blue, and grey and thick", "but it was still quiet". Then it is dark-grey, heaves up from below and smells putrid. Then it boils up in bubbles under a sharp wind. Before the papacy, ships in the distance are pitching and tossing and "firing guns in their sore need", and yet "in the midst of the sky there was still a small bit of blue". The last time the sky is pitch black and the waves rise "as high as church-towers and mountains, and all with crests of white foam at the top". The Low German text says it more strongly: "ene witte Kroon von Schuum" — a white crown of foam. The last crowns in the tale are worn by the waves.
The fisherman sees all of it. He says to himself "It is not right", he thinks "It will not end well" — but he says it to himself, not to his wife, and goes on. His objections stand in brackets too.

Wen links The World to the Gaia Hypothesis — the notion that the world itself "is a living, evolving organism", and that to fulfil one's purpose one "must embrace the spiritual dimension" of one's relationship with the environment. For a couple this reads simply: the shared space between two people is alive, and it responds. For such couples the sea is the shared mood of the home. They have started going to bed later and leaving earlier. Conversations have shrunk to the schedule. The jokes have acquired an edge. They see friends less, because something is always being built at home. In Lisovskaya's book The World in the negative means "Groundhog Day", lots of secrets, isolation from friends and family, and The Wheel in the negative is that very seesaw of silence and quarrels. That is the sea in brackets: it has already changed colour, and nobody has said so out loud.

sections.h2: The trough is not the end of the tale
paragraphs: Everyone remembers how the tale ends: the broken trough. But few notice how it really ends. In Pushkin: "And look: the dugout stands before him again; / On the threshold sits his old woman, / And before her lies the broken trough" (our translation). In the Grimms' version the last sentence is: "Door sitten se noch bet up hüüt un düssen Dag" — **"And there they are living still at this very time"**. They. The two of them.

The Wheel took the palace from the couple, not each other. It returned them not to the end but to the beginning — to the place where they had lived by the sea for thirty-three years and where the fisherman once let the fish go to roam in the open. That is the meaning of the Wheel in its positive aspect: a turn, not a collapse. In Lisovskaya's book such couples change jobs, homes and hobbies together, know how to spot opportunities, accept the partner in any state and feel their meeting was meant to be. Her recommendations sound as if written for the fisherman and his wife: accept change with gratitude, as a reason to move; sometimes let go of control; be generous; ask less of the partner.

The most precise clue to the way out is in Waite, in his description of The World. He writes that the card is "the rapture of the universe when it understands itself in God". In her last wish the fisherman's wife says: "I wish to be like unto God" — in the original "as de lewe Gott". The whole distance of the tail lies between these two sentences. The World is understanding oneself inside the whole. The Wheel in the negative is trying to become the owner of the whole. The 21-4-10 couple enters the task wishing for the first, and halfway along begins demanding the second.

And one last coincidence worth knowing. Philipp Otto Runge, who wrote down the tale of a woman who could not bear to watch the sunrise, spent eight years on the main project of his life — the cycle "Times of Day": morning, day, evening, night. He painted "Morning" in oils twice. The man who passed this story on to us made his life's work exactly what his heroine failed at — watching the sun come up.

sections.h2: Strength at the centre: a clue that is not in the tail
paragraphs: There is no Strength among the tail's three numbers. But a run through every date shows that **every 21-4-10 couple has Strength at a centre** — either at the centre of the couple's own chart or at the centre of one of the two partners. For 75.7% of such couples, the centre of the couple's chart is 11, Strength. For the other 24.3%, the couple's centre is 20, Judgement, and then one of the partners has the personal tail 3-22-19 — and that tail always comes with a personal centre of 11.

The couple's centre is the shared atmosphere, what happens between the two when nobody is watching. In Lisovskaya's book Strength in a couple's atmosphere means they sense finely what the partner needs, charge and strengthen each other, know how to bend and come to terms, and the tension goes into passion. In the negative — a struggle for leadership, "each has their own truth", "different languages". So at the very core of these unions lies exactly the kind of power their middle lacks: mastery of oneself, not of a throne. The Emperor keeps order on the outside; Strength keeps it within.

There is arithmetic tying the centre to the tail as well. With Strength at the centre, the main task plus the atmosphere give the entry: 10 + 11 = 21. Our reading: the Wheel, lived in an atmosphere of Strength, gives the couple back the World they began with.

For couples with Judgement at the centre, the atmosphere rests on something else. In Lisovskaya's book Judgement at the centre means forgiving mistakes, being able to admit one's own, being of equal worth; in the negative — blaming the partner without admitting one's own part, and not being able to say what one feels. In neither version of the tale does either of the two ever say "I was wrong".

sections.h2: The couple's values: the trough and the gain
paragraphs: "The couple's values" is the spiritual purpose, the path the two are to walk together. For 21-4-10 couples only two cards ever stand here: The Lovers for 58.7% and The Devil for 41.3%.

Pushkin, it seems, gave his own hint about what these two cards are arguing over. On getting the new trough, the old woman throws out a pun: "V koryte mnogo l' korysti?" — "How much gain is there in a trough?", where koryto is the trough and korysť is gain, self-interest. The Devil is the card of desire, passion and attraction; in the positive, Lisovskaya means being able to speak openly about one's desires, in the negative — the wish to possess and silence about what one wants. The Lovers is the card of a choice two people make together, and make again. Our reading: in the values, both cards answer the same trouble at the entry. This couple's wish has to be said out loud by both, and to each other — honestly, like The Devil in the positive, and together, like The Lovers. Then the fish has nothing to pass on.

sections.h2: How to calculate the 21-4-10 couple's tail: an example
paragraphs: Each point of the couple's chart is the sum of the same points in the two personal matrices, reduced to 22. Take the dates 5 July 1975 (05.07.1975) and 19 March 1979 (19.03.1979). The partners' personal tails are 12-19-7 and 9-12-3. Add them point by point:

The couple's middle is not recalculated from its edges: it is the sum of the two partners' middles. For this tail it coincides with the reduced sum of the edges — 21 + 10 = 31 → 4 — but that is not how it is calculated.

This couple's centre is 5 + 6 = 11, Strength, and their values are 6, The Lovers. And there is one rarity: The Wheel of Fortune also stands on their "What to create together" point (7 + 3 = 10). That happens for only 6.6% of couples with this tail. What the two met for and their main trial are one and the same card: change is both their gift and their lesson.
What the engine says about the tail as a whole:

ul: **How often.** The 21-4-10 tail occurs in about one couple in 61 (1.643%) — 20th place among the 97 couple tails.
**What it is made of.** Three combinations of personal tails: 12-19-7 + 9-12-3 (48% of such couples), 12-16-4 + 9-15-6 (28%), 18-9-9 + 3-22-19 (24%).

**Whose cards these are.** In 72% of such couples, neither partner has The World, The Emperor or The Wheel in their personal tail. This tail is not inherited from one person — the two of them make it.
**Another order.** Couple's tails made of 21, 4 and 10 in any other order do not exist.

paragraphs: The same order 21-4-10 also occurs as a personal tail — for 3,960 dates since 1900. That is a different calculation with different roles for the points, and it has its own article; texts about the personal tail do not carry over to a couple.
The tail does not set events. It shows where the mechanism most often breaks between two people, so the practices here are about the mechanism.

ul: **Say "we want" to each other, not to the fish.** Before a big step — a move, a purchase, a child, a new job — first say out loud what each of you wants, and only then look for a way to get it. A wish one person carries for two only grows upward.
**Ask not "can we" but "do we both want it".** For the fish the question of what is possible is settled: it can do anything. The tale breaks on another question, the one nobody asks.

**Divide the realm into provinces.** Don't look for who is Kaiser; agree who is responsible for what: the budget, the home, holidays, family. Revisit the rules once they start getting in the way of the people who made them.
**Read the sea out loud.** Notice the "brackets" — shrinking conversations, jokes with an edge, silence after a quarrel — and name them while the sea has only just grown cloudy.
**Don't mistake "let it stay so" for peace.** The wish to freeze a good step is as much a refusal of the Wheel as the wish to command the sunrise.

**Count a return to the start as a turn.** Losing a home, a job, a status or a familiar life takes away the palace, not each other. The question after a turn is not "whose fault is it" but "what do we want now, the two of us".

paragraphs: If the rules in a couple turn into threats, humiliation or fear, this is no longer "the tail's task". In danger, call your local emergency number; with pressure and violence at home, crisis lines and psychologists can help.

ul: **21 · The World — entry to the task.** The couple's shared wish is life in full, with nothing missing: a home, open space, freedom, the feeling that "we have everything". This wish is how the couple enters the task, and the same wish can turn into resistance.
**4 · The Emperor — middle of the task.** The couple's road is construction: rules, division of roles, decisions, hierarchy. Each step reached becomes the floor for the next one.
**10 · The Wheel of Fortune — main task.** The couple's trial is change: rises and falls that obey neither of the two. The task is not to stop the wheel or to command it, but to ride it together.

intro: A couple's tail is neither a forecast nor a verdict. It does not say the two will end up beside a broken trough. It shows the mechanism by which such couples wind up their quarrels and disappointments, and the place where that mechanism can be stopped. What follows is an investigation: clues in the tale, in the cards themselves, in Waite, Wen and Lisovskaya, and in numbers the site's engine has checked against every date.

faq.q: What does the 21-4-10 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is the task of a couple who want life in full together (The World at the entry), build order, rules and roles for it (The Emperor in the middle), and learn the main thing — to accept changes that cannot be commanded (The Wheel of Fortune as the main task). The main trap is trying to hold back or speed up the turn of life instead of going through it together.

faq.q: Is this an unfavourable tail for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not sort unions into lucky and unlucky ones and does not predict events. It shows where conversations between the two most often stumble: on a shared wish that has not been said out loud, on the struggle over who is in charge, and on the attempt to stop or hurry time. Every such couple has Strength at a centre — their own or one partner's — and that is a good resource.

faq.q: Why is The Emperor in the middle if neither of us has it?
faq.a: Because the couple's middle is the sum of the two partners' middles. For 21-4-10 couples the 4 always comes from 31: 19 + 12, 16 + 15 or 9 + 22. Neither partner has The Emperor in the middle of their personal tail: the couple's order and rules are a joint construction, not a habit brought in by one of the two.

faq.q: Can a couple have a tail of the same numbers in a different order?
faq.a: No. A couple's entry is always a multiple of three, so of the numbers 21, 4 and 10 only 21 can stand at the entry. And by the reduction rule the couple's middle "remembers" the sum of the edges: 21 + 10 gives 31 → 4, while the order 21-10-4 would need a 7 or a 16 in the middle.

faq.q: How does the couple's 21-4-10 tail differ from the personal 21-4-10 tail?
faq.a: They are different calculations with different roles for the points. A personal tail is calculated from one date and describes one person's task; a couple's tail is built from two matrices and describes the shared wishes, the shared road and the main trial of the union. Texts about the personal tail do not carry over to a couple.

faq.q: How common is the 21-4-10 tail in couples?
faq.a: About one couple in 61 — 1.643% of all couples, 20th place among the 97 couple tails. Most often it is made of the personal tails 12-19-7 and 9-12-3 (48% of such couples).

The wish to own luck itself, and the turn back — The Wheel of Fortune.

In the tale every step is described in detail: a cottage with hens and a little garden, a castle with crystal chandeliers, and by the throne a row of maids-in-waiting, "each of them always one head shorter than the last", and guards lined up by height, "from the biggest giant, who was two miles high, to the very smallest dwarf, just as big as my little finger". In a modern couple this is the moment when the question of who decides about money, the home, holidays and children gets one answer for everything.
And a clue from the numbers: in such a couple neither of the two has The Emperor in the middle of their personal tail. The empire is not brought in by one person — two people build it.

report.h3: A quarrel not about money, but about time

report: At dawn, already Pope, the fisherman's wife says the main thing: she cannot bear it if she "can't order the sun and moon to rise, and have to look on and see the sun and moon rising". **What is unbearable is watching something turn on its own.** That is The Wheel of Fortune in a single sentence — the couple's main task. The Wheel gives warning, too. The signals are like a stage direction nobody answers. The fisherman himself thinks "It will not end well" — but says it to himself, not to his wife. In a living couple the sea in brackets is conversations shrunk to the schedule, jokes with an edge, silence after a quarrel, friends seen less and less.

report.h3: The trough is not the end

report: Everyone remembers how the tale ends: the broken trough. But in the Grimms' version the last sentence is different: **"And there they are living still at this very time"**. They. The two of them. The Wheel took the palace from the couple, not each other, and returned them not to the end but to the beginning — to where the fish was once let go to roam in the open.

Waite writes of The World as "the rapture of the universe when it understands itself in God". In her last wish the fisherman's wife wants to be "like unto God". The whole distance of the tail lies between these two sentences: The World is understanding oneself inside the whole; The Wheel in the negative is trying to become the owner of the whole.

Such couples have something to lean on. There is no Strength among the tail's numbers, but every 21-4-10 couple has it at a centre — at the centre of the couple's own chart or of one of the two. **Strength is mastery of oneself, not of a throne**: sensing finely what the other needs, coming to terms, knowing how to bend. The way out of the tale looks simple: say "we want" to each other, not to the fish; before a new step, ask not "can we" but "do we both want it"; divide the realm into provinces instead of looking for a single Kaiser; name out loud what stands in brackets while the sea has only just grown cloudy; count a return to the start as a turn, not a verdict.

If the rules in a couple turn into threats, humiliation or fear, this is no longer the tail's task: in danger, call a local emergency number or crisis line; with pressure and violence at home, crisis lines and psychologists can help.

unit.title: Sunrise not to order

captions.M: Want life in full and say so to each other
captions.N: Build order together instead of seeking one Kaiser
captions.D: Neither freeze nor rush change — ride it together

unit.meaning: Your task is to accept change: not to cling to a good step or command the sunrise, but to go through the turns together.
